summary.text: A 22-year-old man with a history of tetralogy of Fallot repair at age two established care after six years without a pediatric cardiology consultation. Holter monitoring showed right bundle branch block and frequent premature ventricular complexes with varying QRS morphologies, there was concern for ventricular arrhythmias, and enalapril 5 mg twice daily was started for left ventricular dysfunction and congestive heart failure.

One year later he had pulmonary valve insufficiency and inducible IART at electrophysiology study. Two months later, at age 24, he underwent pulmonary valve replacement, right ventricular outflow tract reconstruction and a right atrial MAZE procedure, and carvedilol and digoxin were prescribed at discharge. Hemodynamics improved but ventricular ectopy continued; with improved exercise tolerance and no arrhythmia symptoms, the team chose careful observation.

An exercise treadmill test showed 2:1 AV conduction with a ventricular rate of 70 bpm, and an ICD with ATP capabilities and transvenous right atrial and right ventricular leads was placed four months later, with ATP, APP and ARS enabled after X-ray lead confirmation. In the first seven years ATP converted 695 of 956 treated IART episodes (73%), including 630 asymptomatic episodes in one seven-month period; a long QRS interval and poor left ventricular function led to consideration of a biventricular upgrade.

At age 32, generator replacement with a CRT upgrade and a new left ventricular lead was done for battery depletion, with medication changes. One year later his exercise tolerance had improved and the new device had detected no IART. Three months after that the right ventricular lead failed from a microfracture; a three-day hospital stay was needed to remove it, a new CRT-defibrillator system was implanted, and no sustained IART was detected for the next two years.

summary.text: A woman born with dextrotransposition of the great arteries and a ventricular septal defect had a Blalock/Hanlon procedure at two weeks of age and a Mustard atrial switch repair at 2.5 years. At age 29 she presented to the emergency department with palpitations diagnosed as IART, converted with ibultilide, and returned one year later with IART converted with diltiazem; digoxin and benazepril were prescribed.

IART recurred 19 months later and she required four DC cardioversions over four months; procainamide and quinidine did not prevent it. Radiofrequency ablation at age 32 was followed a month later by IART, a fifth cardioversion, and sotalol and warfarin. An electrophysiology study found IART and sinus node dysfunction; the pathway was ablated and a baffle stent placed, but IART recurred three days later and a sixth cardioversion produced a junctional rhythm.

At age 33 an AT500 pacemaker with transvenous leads was placed and ATP enabled; the device recognized IART immediately and converted it on the second attempt, APP and ARS were enabled, and sotalol was discontinued. She later stopped warfarin and halved digoxin. The first device converted 31 of 31 treated episodes over five years, and an EnRhythm generator then converted 101 of 105 in its first five years.

One IART episode at age 43 persisted despite 20 ATP sequences and ended spontaneously. At age 46 a sustained episode with 1:1 conduction led to bisoprolol, digoxin withdrawal and generator replacement with an Advisa system. Incision-site pain and subcutaneous fat thinning led to pocket revision, and no sustained IART was documented for two years. Over about 16 years 333 of 348 episodes (96%) were converted.

summary.text: A man with double inlet left ventricle and levotransposition of the great arteries had pulmonary banding at six weeks and an atriopulmonary Fontan procedure at age eight. At age 14 he presented with a syncopal episode and near-syncope, and a week later had near-syncope with a heart rate of 35 bpm. Holter monitoring showed junctional rhythms with bradycardia and no arrhythmia episodes, and catheterization found adequate Fontan pressures.

Lost to follow-up for seven years, he returned at age 21 after two symptomatic IART episodes, had two more needing cardioversions, and then lost consciousness with IART requiring DC cardioversion. Atenolol and an electrophysiology study with ablation followed, but IART recurred repeatedly despite higher atenolol and then sotalol, with noncompliance and nausea and headaches at a higher sotalol dose. A second study ablated two circuits, IART recurred five hours later, and amiodarone was prescribed.

Fontan conversion, right-sided maze, right atrial reduction plasty, septectomy and temporary epicardial pacing leads were followed by IART treated with overdrive pacing and then an AT500 pacemaker with ATP and APP enabled. The device failed to convert IART at one month and again two months later because 1:1 AV conduction disabled ATP; the ventricular lead was capped and the device reprogrammed, after which 347 of 357 episodes (97%) were converted, although ED visits for undetected or resistant IART continued.

Generator changes at age 30 (EnRhythm) and age 35 (Advisa) followed battery depletion; undetected IART episodes and medication compliance problems persisted, with some episodes needing overdrive pacing or cardioversion. The second device converted 44 of 46 detected episodes, and the first year of the third device converted 13 of 13. Over about 13 years, 404 of 416 episodes (97%) were converted by ATP.
